doc.title: Wendy Oxenhorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 22, 2026

title: Raising money and counselling musicians through home visits
summary: Asked how the Great Night in Harlem came about, she explains musicians were too proud to ask, and describes helping them by visiting homes and buying groceries.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Did it occur to you that maybe the best way to support these veteran musicians who had some troubles was to reach out to the musicians who were doing fairly well and could help out?
Well I’m wondering, if you had came up with the Great Night in Harlem and how did that idea come to you?

Oh well you know I knew we needed a lot of money. I started seeing that the musicians were really in a bad way and because they were so proud, no one would ever come and ask for help. You had to hear someone was having a hard time through someone else. So © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

I was – you know I knew nothing really about jazz. And I didn’t have, I mean I left school for the ballet, I left school after ninth grade. That was the highest education I had. So I, you know there weren’t like research studies I did on helping people, I had not become a licensed social worker, but my time at the hotline, the suicide hotline, I had been counseling for years and I had a few other organizations not just helping the homeless but kids and people in rough situations. So I had a lot of counseling experience. And I was very intuitive. So it was easy to know how to help the musicians because they thought like me. You know? They were all living on the fringe for years, they were very resourceful, they were creative, and they always thought outside the box. So finding ways to help them was so easy for both of us. Because they knew, you know I was very clear in the fact that I had been at one point living on eight dollars a day with two kids. You know? When I was starting my charities in the past I didn’t have family money to back it up, I was just going raw, just like they do for the love of what they do so they could see that I really, genuinely had been in their position and I really understood. So I was able to say to them, “I’m buying you groceries today and you’re going to accept it, because, you know, and then we would laugh later that night when I’d call them and they’d be eating, you know, tuna fish sandwiches when they had just had a jar of pickles in the fridge and a bunch of ketchup packets. You know and the only reason I knew was ‘cause I would go to their homes. You know they never tell you anything like really, so the only way to really discover how someone’s doing would be to go visit them. And you’d have a great excuse, “I was in the ‘hood taking care of someone else” which was good. That meant that I’m not there just for them so they don’t feel like they’re a charitable case you know. I was there and we had such a great talk on the phone I just wanted to come by and say hello and I remembered you said sardines you loved so I brought some. You know? And the door opened and we would talk for an hour, and then I would just happen to get myself something from the fridge, and say, “Oh I’m just going to grab something” you know some water or ice cubes or whatever. And then I’d get to see what was in it. And then I’d get to really go shopping and we’d get to make a list of what they wanted and I would tell them I went through the same thing and someone did this for me so I’m just passing it on and I’m going to do it for you. You know and it was just – there was a soul connection that was truly magical and beautiful. And what was so ironic was a lot of these people were the people that my love affair that he used to take me to hear, these were his idols. So I learned about some of them before, even though I knew nothing about jazz I learned by going. You know? And hearing. Being taken to hear somebody.
